extracted.intended_audience: poets and satirists composing verse (writers of poetic satire)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for composing effective satirical verse: tone, metrical craft, audience, moral limits, and revision work specific to satire/poetry. Geared to poets who wish to shape satiric content and poetic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality over quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Not writing MUCH; for that I grant you. See, Here comes Crispinus ... writing WELL, Not writing MUCH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing copious fluent lines at the expense of craft. Lucilius is criticised for pouring forth 'two hundred verses in an hour' and leaving 'a load of refuse' behind: prefer careful composition and finished lines rather than sheer volume. The anti-pattern is the 'bellows' that puffs out windy nothings to seem profound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and pruning
rubrics_metrics.description: You must draw your pen not once nor twice but o'er and o'er again Through what you've written, if you would entice The man that reads you once to read you twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly edit and 'apply the file' to excrescences; prune redundancies and excessive phrasing. Horace pictures the labor of cutting and polishing a poem (bite your nails till they bled) as necessary to make readers return. Quick composition without revision is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terseness and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Terseness there wants, to make the thought ring clear, Nor with a crowd of words confuse the ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise expression so ideas 'ring clear'. Avoid confusing the ear with a crowd of words; terseness sharpens wit and makes satire effective. The anti-pattern is verbose circumlocution that buries the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of tone and a plastic style
rubrics_metrics.description: There wants a plastic style, now grave, now light, Now such as bard or orator would write, And now the language of a well-bred man, Who masks his strength, and says not all he can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a flexible, 'plastic' style that shifts between grave and light registers, sometimes oratorical, sometimes colloquial. Masking strength and restraint (saying less than you can) increases force. Avoid a monotonous single tone; cultivate range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cadence and metrical music (poetry vs prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strip what I write ... Of cadence and succession, time and note, ... no poetry you'll find: but break up this ... still The bard remains, unlimb him as you will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain rhythm, cadence, and musical arrangement; poetry is not merely prose in metre. If you remove cadence and musical ordering, the work ceases to be poetry. Attention to metrical flow and succession of sounds is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal malice and defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: He who maligns an absent friend's fair fame, Who says no word for him when others blame, ... Beware him, Roman! that man steals or stabs!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use satire as a vehicle for vindictive slander against absent friends. Horace condemns the gratuitous malicious lampoon that merely courts a laugh; the ethical line is emphasized with examples of poison-bag detraction. Prefer measured moral critique over personal vitriol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at a discerning audience, not mob-pleasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Not making popular applause your cue, But looking to fit audience, although few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for the intelligent, tasteful readers whose praise matters (friends, peers), rather than pandering to the hooting mob. Horace values the approval of select critics (Maecenas, Virgil, Varius) over popular applause. Anti-pattern: tailoring verse solely for wide, vulgar popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject to genre and appropriate muse
rubrics_metrics.description: No; keep that name for genius, for a soul Of Heaven's own fire, ... Some have questioned if the Muse we call The Comic Muse be really one at all: Her subject ne'er aspires, her style ne'er glows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the right genre for your subject — satire has its own appropriate style and limitations; do not force comic/satiric treatment into forms or subjects better served by epic, tragic, or other modes. Know which 'Muse' suits your subject and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of linguistic register (avoid unsuitable mixing)
rubrics_metrics.description: But surely that's a merit quite unique, His gift of mixing Latin up with Greek, ... Or would you practise it, when called to plead For poor Petillius, at his direst need?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of mixing registers or languages (hybrid Latin-Greek) in contexts where purity of diction is required — e.g., legal or serious contexts. Novel linguistic tricks may be graceful in some settings but inappropriate or distracting in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion in moral judgement and satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Why should not reason use her own just sense, And square her punishments to each offence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat faults and crimes with due proportion: don't equate minor lapses with grave offences simply to make a point. Sense, custom, and expedience demand discriminating treatment; caricaturing all vices alike undermines moral credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion about public airing and recitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Others are less fastidious: some will air Their last production in the public square: ... Weak brains, to whom the question ne'er occurred If what they do be vain, ill-timed, absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be tactful about when and where you present satiric work. Publicly thrusting out every fresh production is poor taste; prefer measured, appropriate occasions and private circulation among friends if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pleasantry and humour to dissolve gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: And pleasantry will often cut clean through Hard knots that gravity would scarce undo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply humour and lightness as a tool to resolve complex, knotty moral or rhetorical problems that gravity alone cannot untangle. Wit, properly applied, can make critique more effective than sheer severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong, clear character portrayal (comic tradition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cratinus, Aristophanes, and all The elder comic poets ... Portrayed him without fear in strong relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the comic tradition of bold, clear depiction of folly and vice: portray characters in strong relief so that their faults are recognizable and instructive. But pair bold depiction with craft and restraint (see other criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in invective (balance biting wit with restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some think in satire I'm too keen, and press The spirit of invective to excess: Some call my verses nerveless: once begin, A thousand such per day a man might spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance sharpness and restraint: satire should bite but not devolve into aimless bitter invective or, conversely, into timidity that makes it 'nerveless.' Calibrate severity to subject, audience, and moral purpose.
